input: The affinity laws are a set of useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its rotational speed is varied. Essentially, these laws express three proportionalities connecting speed to the main performance variables. Firstly, the flow is directly proportional to the speed, meaning that doubling the speed doubles the flow. Secondly, the head is proportional to the square of the speed, so doubling the speed increases the head fourfold. Thirdly, the power is proportional to the cube of the speed, which means that doubling the speed increases the power eightfold. A simple worked check helps to illustrate these relationships clearly. When the speed is increased by a factor of 2, the flow increases by a factor of 2, the head by a factor of 4, and the power by a factor of 8. This striking result highlights why even modest increases in speed can have such a dramatic effect on power consumption in practice. It is important to remember, however, that these laws apply to the same pump handling the same liquid, and that they describe how the pump curve itself shifts with speed rather than how the wider system responds, which is an important distinction to bear in mind when applying them. Moreover, because the laws are expressed as ratios, they can be applied without reference to the absolute size of the machine in question, a feature that makes them especially convenient for quick estimates and preliminary assessments of proposed operating changes.
target:
The affinity laws state how the duty of a centrifugal pump changes when its rotational speed changes and the pump geometry stays fixed. The laws give three proportionalities, one each for flow, head and power. Flow is proportional to speed. Head is proportional to the square of speed. Power is proportional to the cube of speed. Each proportionality compares the pump with itself at a second speed, so the ratios carry no units and need no pump data beyond the speed change itself.

The worked check takes a doubling of speed. At a speed ratio of 2, the flow ratio is 2, the head ratio is 4 and the power ratio is 8. The power figure governs the cost of a speed increase: a pump driven twice as fast draws eight times the power, while delivering twice the flow against four times the head. The same ratios run in reverse, and a reduction in speed cuts the power far faster than it cuts the flow, which is the basis of variable-speed control of pumping duty. The laws are stated for the same pump and the same liquid, at operation near the duty point. They describe the pump curve shifting with speed, not a change in the system the pump works against. Where the system resistance is mostly static lift rather than friction, the operating point moves off the affinity path, and the ratios alone no longer fix the new duty. The check also shows why the affinity laws are ratios before they are numbers: the same check at any other speed change returns the speed ratio raised to the first, second and third powers in turn.
